c2be53701f:
This chapter is about how one agent becomes a team without turning into a mess. It covers the hub-and-spoke topology and what a subagent can and cannot see. It shows how the Task tool spawns a subagent, how an AgentDefinition shapes it, and how to write the brief it receives.

From there it moves to the coordinator's work: how to decompose and partition the job, run subagents in parallel, refine in rounds, and handle failures as they travel back. It ends with branching a session through a fork.

Everything is built from first principles on top of the loop in chapter 01, with traces of real message shapes. Implementations are in Python and Java/Spring.
3212ada9a2:
The whole topic collapses into two sentences.

A multi-agent system is several of the loops from chapter 01, in which one loop (the coordinator) owns the task and treats the others (subagents) as tools: it decomposes the request, writes each subagent a self-contained brief, receives only each subagent's final message, and merges the results; subagents start with empty memory, never talk to each other, and know only what the brief says.

The mechanism is ordinary tool use: the coordinator's response contains one or more tool_use blocks named Task (allowed only if "Task" is in its allowed tools), each carrying a prompt, and the harness answers each with a tool_result holding the subagent's last message, so the quality of the whole system is decided by three things you control: how the coordinator splits the work, what it writes into each prompt, and what format the answers come back in.
4fc744c700:
Everything else follows from those two sentences.

Hub-and-spoke exists because the coordinator is the only component that sees every handoff. So it's the only place where failures can be handled and traces can be read.

Context isolation cuts both ways. It's the reason subagents are worth having: each one gets a clean window. It's also the reason they're dangerous: each one forgets everything you didn't write down.

Take the official sample about AI in creative industries. Every subagent succeeds, and the report still covers only visual art. That's a decomposition failure, and no amount of work on the subagents repairs it.

The parallelism rule (several Task calls in one response) is the pairing rule you met in chapter 01. It just applies to a tool whose handler happens to be another model loop.

The fork material in task 1.3 is the one piece about sessions rather than subagents. It's easiest to understand once you've seen that a session is nothing more than a saved message history.
604642fd6a:
The two task statements list their knowledge points as follows.

1.2:

  • the hub-and-spoke architecture, in which the coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling and information routing;
  • subagents operate with isolated context and don't automatically inherit the coordinator's history;
  • the coordinator's role in task decomposition, delegation, result aggregation and deciding which subagents to invoke;
  • the risk of overly narrow decomposition, with the official example of a creative-industries report that covers only visual arts.

1.3:

  • the Task tool as the spawning mechanism, and the need for allowedTools to include "Task";
  • subagent context passed explicitly in the prompt;
  • the AgentDefinition configuration (description, system prompt, tool restrictions);
  • fork-based session management.

The skills listed with them are the checklist for the second half of this chapter:

  • select subagents dynamically by query complexity;
  • partition scope to minimise duplication;
  • run iterative refinement loops that evaluate gaps and re-delegate;
  • route all communication through the coordinator for observability;
  • include complete prior findings in subagent prompts;
  • use structured formats that separate content from metadata;
  • spawn in parallel with multiple Task calls in one response;
  • write prompts that give goals and quality criteria instead of procedures.

Each one is taught with a trace you can run.
78543d1e70:
Dividing a problem among specialists who report to a manager is older than computing. Two things are new in the LLM era. Each specialist is a model with a context window instead of a process with a call stack. And the briefs are written in natural language.

Tracing the lineage explains why the exam keeps asking the same questions: who talks to whom, and who owns the plan.
4fea9e2dc3:
Early speech-understanding research at Carnegie Mellon produced the blackboard architecture (Hearsay-II, mid-1970s). Several independent knowledge sources (acoustic, lexical, syntactic) read from and wrote to a shared structure. A scheduler decided which one ran next. It's a peer-style design: specialists coordinate through shared state rather than through a manager.

At about the same time, Hewitt and colleagues described the actor model (1973). Actors are independent units with private state that communicate only by asynchronous messages.

Both ideas matter here because they're the two roads agent frameworks later took, and the exam's choice between them is deliberate. A shared blackboard that every agent can read and write is choreography through state. An actor that receives a message, works in private and replies is a spoke.
dfbc5f371c:
Reid Smith's contract net protocol (1980) is the direct ancestor of delegation. A manager announces a task, contractors bid, the manager awards it, and the contractor returns a result. The roles are asymmetric on purpose. The manager decomposes and awards; the contractor executes and reports.

The 1990s turned this into a field, multi-agent systems, with standards such as the FIPA agent communication language (the FIPA body was founded in 1996). FIPA specified message types between peer agents. Peer messaging was expressive, but in practice it was hard to debug. When ten agents negotiate directly, nobody owns the transcript.

Industry quietly kept the manager-worker shape instead: batch schedulers, job queues, and later MapReduce (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004). In MapReduce one master splits the input, assigns map tasks, collects results and reassigns the ones that failed.

If you've run Spring Batch with partitioned steps, you've used this pattern. A manager step creates partitions. Worker steps run them in isolation. The manager aggregates and decides what to do about failures.
f99217bafb:
The microservices decade made the trade-off explicit. In choreography, each service reacts to events from others, and no component knows the whole flow. In orchestration, one component (a saga orchestrator, or a workflow engine such as Camunda or Temporal) owns the flow and calls the others.

Choreography scales across teams, and it's miserable to trace and change. Orchestration puts the logic in one place.

Telecom order management lives on this trade-off every day. An order that touches billing, provisioning and inventory needs one place that can answer "where is it stuck and what do we compensate". Hold that picture. The hub-and-spoke rule in 1.2 is the same argument, applied to a set of non-deterministic services.
2720356a11:
Once a single model could run a tool loop (chapter 01), people put several in one program. Park et al.'s Generative Agents (2023) simulated a town of model-driven characters that talked to each other. Microsoft's AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023) and CAMEL let agents converse in groups. MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023) assigned software-company roles (product manager, architect, engineer) that handed documents down a pipeline.

Most of these were peer conversations or fixed pipelines. They produced striking demos and unpredictable bills. Agents talked in circles and repeated each other's work. When something went wrong, the evidence was spread across several private transcripts.

In late 2024, Anthropic's Building effective agents essay described an orchestrator-workers workflow. A central model breaks a task into parts it couldn't have listed in advance, delegates them to worker calls, and synthesises the results. That's the pattern this chapter is about. The essay also advises keeping designs simple and adding structure only when it measurably helps, and that's the right prior.
084e159378:
Claude Code shipped subagents: named specialists that the main session can launch through a built-in tool. Each one is defined in a Markdown file with a description, a tool list and a system prompt. The same harness became the Claude Agent SDK, which lets you define subagents in code with an AgentDefinition and spawn them from your own coordinator.

Anthropic also published an account of its own multi-agent research system. It uses an orchestrator-worker design: a lead agent plans and spawns parallel search subagents. Anthropic reported that it beat a single agent on its internal research evaluation, while using several times more tokens (check the post for the current figures).

The lessons it draws are, almost word for word, this exam's skills list:

  • Teach the lead how to delegate, with a clear objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries for each subagent. Vague briefs produced duplicated work and gaps.
  • Scale the number of subagents to the complexity of the query.
  • Run independent searches in parallel.

Other practitioners offered a counterpoint the same year, and it's worth knowing. They argued that parallel subagents working from partial context make conflicting implicit decisions. For tightly coupled work such as code changes, one agent with a shared context is more reliable.

This chapter takes both seriously. Use subagents for separable, breadth-first work, and pay the explicit price of writing context into every brief.
ae47aa14a5: Before building a team, be clear about what a team fixes. A single agent with every tool and every document runs into three limits. Each one has a mechanical cause you can point at.
5b8f22699a:
From chapter 01: the history is resent on every call, and the model attends to all of it. A research task makes this worse than a support task, because the tool results are large. A fetched page is thousands of tokens, and perhaps two sentences of it matter.

After eight searches, the window holds eight pages of navigation text and cookie banners. Every later call pays for them again, and has to find the relevant sentences among them.

Two effects follow. Cost grows with the square of the number of calls, as in chapter 01 section 07. And quality degrades before the window is full, because the instructions and the key facts compete for attention with a lot of irrelevant text.

A subagent is a way to throw the noise away. It reads the eight pages in its own window, and what returns to the parent is a short structured answer.
297addcfc8:
Every tool definition is part of the prompt, and the model chooses among tools by reading their descriptions. With four well-separated tools, the choice is easy. With eighteen overlapping tools, the model picks the wrong one more often. The descriptions also become a large fixed cost on every turn. Chapter 06 covers the evidence and the fix: fewer, scoped tools per role.

Subagents are the structural version of that fix. The web researcher has one search tool. The analyst has one warehouse tool. The synthesizer has a write tool. None of them can misuse the others' tools, because none of them has those tools.
9a0b4f4417:
A single loop makes its tool calls one turn after another. Parallel tool calls in one turn help, but only when the model knows in advance which calls are independent. So a question that needs five separate lines of investigation takes five times as long as one.

Subagents run in separate loops, and the coordinator can start all of them from one response. Wall-clock time is then set by the slowest investigation instead of the sum.
6b001c4793:
There's no special runtime object. A subagent is a second tool loop, started by a tool call from the first. It has a new empty messages list, its own system prompt, and its own subset of tools.

When it ends (stop_reason: "end_turn"), its final text becomes the content of a tool_result in the parent's history. Nothing else crosses back. From the coordinator's side, delegating is exactly like calling any other tool. This one just happens to take a long time and return a paragraph.

Companion example 02_task_tool_spawn.py prints the two loops side by side. You'll read its trace in section 07.
492515d7f7:
The price is that nothing is shared for free. The clean window that makes a subagent useful is also what makes it ignorant. It doesn't know the user's request, the constraint the user stated, or what the previous round found, unless you wrote it into the prompt.

Most of the failures in this chapter are one of two kinds. Either the coordinator split the work badly (the decomposition failures of section 09). Or it wrote a brief that left out something the subagent needed (the context failures of sections 05 and 08).
910e1fbb19:
There are four ways to wire several agents together. The exam wants you to recognise why only one of them is the answer.

  • In a pipeline, agent A's output is agent B's input, fixed in advance. That's a workflow. It's fine when the stages are known (extract, validate, summarise), but nobody decides what to do when a stage returns something unexpected.
  • In a peer-to-peer design, agents message each other directly.
  • In a shared blackboard design, they read and write a common store.
  • In hub-and-spoke, a coordinator talks to each subagent, and the subagents talk only to the coordinator.
ab5c89cb92:
The official task statement names three benefits of routing everything through the coordinator. Each is something you can demonstrate rather than assert.

  • Observability: every brief and every result passes through one component. One log answers "what did we ask, what came back, in what order".
  • Consistent error handling: one place decides whether a failed subagent is retried, replaced by another, or reported as a labelled gap.
  • Controlled information flow: the coordinator decides what each subagent is told. An unverified claim from one subagent doesn't silently become the premise of another.

Companion example 18_antipattern_peer_to_peer.py builds the contrast. In the peer-to-peer version, agent A crashes. Agent B waits for A's notes, times out, and assumes pricing is irrelevant. The synthesizer reports that "network is the main driver". The only evidence of the failure sits in A's private log.

In the hub version, the failure arrives at the coordinator as a structured result. The coordinator retries once or reports the gap. Section 12 shows the trace.
def0bcbe25:
The cost is real, and the exam doesn't hide it. Every handoff is two hops, and the coordinator becomes the place where information gets summarised.

If the coordinator paraphrases a subagent's findings before passing them on, claims and sources drift apart. This is the telephone game. It's why section 08 insists that findings travel as structured records, and that the coordinator forwards them verbatim to the synthesizer.

The other cost: the coordinator's decomposition becomes a single point of failure for coverage. That's the subject of section 09.
ab9d8c8034:
The task statement names four responsibilities: decomposition, delegation, aggregation, and selective invocation. It helps to see them as the stages of a Spring Batch job with partitioned steps.

  • The manager step partitions the input into ranges (decomposition).
  • It starts a worker step for each partition, with its own execution context (delegation).
  • When the workers finish, it aggregates their results and decides what to do about partitions that failed (aggregation).
  • And a well-designed job doesn't partition a ten-row table into ten workers (selective invocation).

The difference is who does the partitioning. In Spring, the partitioner is code you wrote. Here, it's a model reasoning about a question it has never seen. That's why each job needs an explicit instruction in the coordinator's system prompt.
a2ec4ef707:
Read that prompt as a specification of the four jobs. Lines 1 to 2 are decomposition and selective invocation. Lines 3 to 5 are delegation. Lines 6 to 7 are aggregation and refinement.

Exam questions about coordinator behaviour almost always have a wrong option that tries to fix a coordinator problem somewhere else: a bigger model for the subagents, more instructions to the synthesizer. But the coordinator's behaviour lives in the prompt.
93eca62688:
A subagent starts with three things: the system prompt from its definition, its allowed tools, and one user message. That message holds whatever the coordinator wrote in the Task prompt.

It doesn't see the coordinator's system prompt, the user's original message, the coordinator's earlier tool results, earlier rounds, or any sibling's output.

The official statement is that subagents "do not automatically inherit" the coordinator's history. The word automatically carries the design rule. Inheritance is possible only by writing the information into the prompt.
b4855afb23: Companion example 01_isolation.py makes this concrete. The coordinator's context contains a user request with a CFO constraint ("only sources published after 2025-06") and round-1 findings about visual art. It delegates twice in one response. The first prompt is the kind a human writes to a colleague who was in the meeting:
aebae0ac1f:
Look at the two sentences in prompt A. "The gaps from before" refers to a conversation the subagent never saw. "What we found" refers to findings it doesn't have. "The CFO's date constraint" names a rule without stating it.

The scripted subagent here returns a labelled gap ("brief gave no sub-area; cannot tell what to research"). That's the best a careful agent can do. A real model is more likely to guess. It'll pick a plausible interpretation, search for it, and return confident findings about something the coordinator didn't ask for.

Both outcomes cost a full subagent run, and the second one is silent.

This is also why the exam's wrong answers in this area are wrong: "the subagent can look up the earlier findings", "subagents share a memory store with the coordinator". Nothing in the platform provides that automatically.
b22cc83dbf:
Only the subagent's final message returns to the coordinator, as the content of the tool_result. The searches it ran, the pages it read, and its intermediate reasoning aren't in the coordinator's history. That's the whole benefit, since the coordinator's window stays small. It has two consequences.

First, the final message must be the complete deliverable, in a format the coordinator can use without asking a question back. A subagent that ends with "I found several sources, let me know if you want details" has delivered nothing.

Second, anything not in the final message is lost: the page number the subagent saw in a tool result, the URL of the page it summarised. If provenance is needed downstream, the output format must demand it. That's the subject of section 08.
c42073509d:
It's fair to ask why the platform doesn't just copy the parent's history into each subagent. There are four reasons, in rough order of importance.

  • Cost: a coordinator that has built up 40,000 tokens would hand each of ten subagents 40,000 tokens it mostly doesn't need. That multiplies the quadratic cost of chapter 01 by ten.
  • Noise: the point of a subagent is a clean window focused on one question.
  • Safety and least information: a subagent that sees only its brief can't be misled by an injected instruction in a tool result the coordinator read earlier. And it can't leak a constraint it was never told.
  • Predictability: if the input is one string, you can log it, test it and replay it.

Sometimes you do want a subagent-like worker to start from an existing history. Then you don't spawn; you fork a session, which is section 13. The distinction is precise: spawn for a clean start, fork for a copy of what has been done.
1c2ac547b1:
Two details need care, because they vary by version and surface.

First, whether a subagent also loads project-level instruction files (for example CLAUDE.md) or other settings depends on the runtime and configuration. Check the docs for your version before relying on either behaviour.

Second, the Claude Code docs, as I read them at the time of writing, say that subagents can't spawn further subagents (check the current docs). So the hierarchy is one level deep. The companion harness enforces the same rule, and example 03_allowed_tools_task.py shows the refusal.
b576569d24:
In Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK, a coordinator starts a subagent by calling a built-in tool. The exam guide calls it the Task tool.

Recent Claude Code releases display the same tool as the Agent tool. The docstrings in the current Python SDK (version 0.2.164, which I checked while writing this chapter) say "invokable via the Agent tool". Treat the two names as one mechanism. Answer "Task" on the exam, and check the docs for how permission rules spell it in your version.

At the time of writing, its input carries three fields: which subagent type to start, a short description for logs, and the prompt. The model decides when to call it the same way it decides to call any tool.

Two properties of the tool matter for design. First, its description is assembled from the descriptions of the available subagents. So an AgentDefinition's description is routing text: it's how the coordinator decides which subagent a sub-task belongs to.

Second, because it's a tool, everything from chapter 01 applies. The call arrives as a tool_use block with an id. The harness must return a tool_result with that id. And several Task blocks in one response are legal (section 10).
98968be600:
Spawning is a tool call, so it's subject to the permission rules that govern every tool call. A coordinator whose allowed tools are ["Read", "Grep"] will never delegate, however clearly its prompt says to.

The model may try to call Task and be refused, or never be offered it. Either way the work stays in one agent, and the symptom is a coordinator that "just answers by itself". Companion example 03_allowed_tools_task.py runs the same scripted coordinator twice:
bbe2abb8ea:
A nuance, because the field name suggests more than it does. In the current SDKs, allowed_tools is a permission list. Tools named in it are approved without asking. Anything not approved falls to the permission mode, and in a headless run with nobody to ask, that means it's denied.

The base set of tools that exist at all is configured separately. The Python options also have tools and disallowed_tools; check the docs for the exact interplay in your version.

For the exam, the rule is simple: if the scenario says the coordinator never launches subagents, check that "Task" is in its allowed tools before touching any prompt.

The reverse direction is a design rule: don't give subagents the Task tool. It breaks the one-level hierarchy, hides handoffs from the coordinator, and lets a cheap model spawn work recursively.
542985eee7: A subagent type is described by an AgentDefinition. The four fields the task statement lists are the ones that matter for the exam. The current Python SDK defines more, and I list them from the installed class so you know they exist.
03d9189bde:
The installed Python SDK's dataclass has these further fields, which I'm listing from its source rather than from memory: disallowedTools, skills, memory, mcpServers, initialPrompt, maxTurns, background, effort and permissionMode.

Two are worth remembering for design. maxTurns is a per-subagent budget, the kind chapter 01 section 13 calls a circuit breaker. mcpServers scopes MCP tools to one subagent. That's how you give the warehouse analyst a database tool the web researcher never sees. Exact semantics evolve, so check the docs.
ec6346e133: The definition below is the one the companion examples use. Look at what's absent as much as what's present. No subagent has Task. The researcher can't query the warehouse. The synthesizer can't search.
d30d3b585e:
The same definitions can live in files. In Claude Code, a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter defines a subagent. It goes under .claude/agents/ (shared through git) or ~/.claude/agents/ (personal). The frontmatter carries the name, description, tools and model, and the body is the system prompt.

The /agents command manages them interactively. Check the docs for which location wins when names collide.
d510370420:
A last point on tool restriction as a safety property. The harness enforces the restriction; it doesn't rely on the subagent's good manners.

In example 03, part C, a scripted web researcher tries to call query_warehouse. The harness answers with an is_error result ("Tool 'query_warehouse' is not available to this agent"), and the trace records a denial.

This is the same idea as hooks in chapter 03. A rule that must hold is enforced where the call is executed, not requested in the prompt.
48a1dd3ecc:
Now trace a complete delegation through the wire format, using companion example 02_task_tool_spawn.py. The user asks about AI in the games industry, and the coordinator delegates one sub-area.

First, the coordinator's request carries a Task tool in its tools list. Its schema's subagent_type enum lists the available subagents. The response comes back with stop_reason: "tool_use":
91e7598db4:
Nothing here is new. It's a text block plus a tool_use block, exactly the shape of chapter 01.

What the harness does next is the new part. It looks up web-researcher in the agent definitions. It creates a new messages list whose only entry is the prompt string. It calls the Messages API with the definition's system prompt, tool list and model. Then it runs the chapter-01 loop to completion.

The trace the companion harness writes shows both loops (ms are wall-clock; the search tool sleeps 150 ms to imitate latency):
4c4c2fbf7f: Read it as nested loops. The coordinator's turn 1 ends with tool_use. A subagent loop runs inside the handler, with two model turns: search, then answer. From the coordinator's point of view, the whole thing is a single tool execution that took 154 ms. Then the coordinator's turn 2 begins, and its request contains the Task result:
03a2b24a0b:
The pairing rule is unchanged. The tool_use_id of the result equals the id of the Task call, and the example asserts it. The result is a string (JSON here, because the subagent was told to return JSON).

The coordinator now sees 635 characters instead of the page text the subagent read. It continues its own loop on stop_reason, exactly as before. Everything in chapter 01 about stop reasons, budgets and idempotence applies to both loops, independently.
9773027404:
The Task prompt is the subagent's entire world (section 05). Writing it well is most of the craft of orchestration.

The task statement lists three skills for it: include complete prior findings, use structured formats that separate content from metadata, and specify goals and quality criteria rather than procedures. A fourth, spawning in parallel, gets its own section. This section takes the three in turn, then assembles them into one template.
7161d901c3:
When a later subagent needs what an earlier one found (verification, extension, synthesis), the coordinator must paste those findings into the new prompt. "Complete" has two meanings.

Complete in coverage: every finding relevant to that subagent's task, not a hand-picked sample. The subagent can't ask for the rest.

Complete in detail: the claim with its source, not a one-line summary. The next step (verify this claim, extend this source, merge these figures) needs the source to do its job.

A summary written by the coordinator is a second, lossy copy. If it drops the page number or rounds 1.4 to "about 1", the error now sits upstream of every later step.
502e7ad015: Example 10_iterative_refinement.py shows the right shape. In round 2, the coordinator re-delegates only the sub-areas with gaps. Each brief carries what's already known, inside delimiters the subagent can recognise:
18e9a596a2:
The scripted researcher echoes how many prior findings it received (prior_findings_seen). That's a test double's way of proving the information arrived. A real subagent uses the findings to avoid repeating the search and to look for new sources.

Two practical rules. First, put the findings in a delimited block, not in running prose. The subagent can then tell data from instruction, and a stray sentence inside a retrieved document is less likely to be read as an order.

Second, watch the size. Ten findings are cheap; ten thousand aren't. When the set is large, pass the records relevant to that subagent's sub-area, not the whole store. Completeness is about relevance, not volume.
a08c4ea353: The second skill is about the shape of what comes back, because the format a subagent returns decides whether provenance survives. Here's what the researchers in a research system typically return when no format is specified:
f283c0ee6d:
From these, a synthesizer can't produce a single citation. There's no URL, no document name, no page. The two mentions of 1.4% might be one source or two. "Another report" can't be followed. The synthesizer was told "cite your sources", and it has nothing to cite.

This is exactly the situation in the second worked scenario at the end of the chapter. It's also why pushing the synthesizer harder is the wrong fix. The loss happened upstream, where the format was chosen.

The fix is to make each finding a record in which the claim is one field and its metadata are other fields:
04bae94301:
Records like this can be validated, merged and rendered by code, with no model involved. That's where you want mechanical work to happen. Example 11_structured_findings.py does three things with them.

  • It validates a batch. Every finding needs a claim and a source with title, URL, publisher and date; page may be null, but the key must exist. The coordinator can send a failing batch back to the subagent.
  • It deduplicates by URL. Five records from two batches become four findings, because one source was found twice.
  • It flags conflicts. Two findings with the same metric and different values are shown side by side with their sources, instead of one being chosen silently.
15162e9a56:
Three details matter beyond the demo.

First, provenance fields are chosen by what a reader needs to find the source again: document name or title, URL, page number or section, publication date, and for internal data the table name and date range. The task statement's list is "URLs, document names, page numbers". Add the date, because two versions of a document with the same title are common.

Second, the format is a contract, and it belongs in the subagent's definition. Its system prompt carries the schema, so every Task prompt doesn't have to repeat it.

Third, for extra reliability, have the subagent return the record through a tool with a JSON Schema instead of as free text. Then the API enforces the structure rather than merely requesting it. Chapter 12 covers that technique, along with validation and retry loops for the cases where it still fails.
5f0aa00848: The same principle applies to the coordinator's own handoff. When it sends findings to the synthesizer, it forwards the records verbatim. If it rewrites them into a paragraph first, it has re-created the prose problem one level up.
5779f8521f: The third skill is about the instruction part of the brief. A procedural brief tells the subagent which steps to take. A goal-and-criteria brief tells it what a good result looks like, and leaves the steps to the subagent. Compare the two forms from example 12_goal_vs_procedure_prompts.py:
ee37aafb32:
Why is the second better? Look at what the subagent is: a capable model with a tool loop of its own. It sees search results the coordinator hasn't seen. It can notice that the first five results are blog posts, that the useful source is on page two, or that "FWA churn" is called "fixed-wireless attrition" in filings.

A procedure assumes none of that happens. It fails the first time the world differs from the plan. And it fails silently, because the subagent did what it was told.

A goal with criteria survives the difference. The criteria give the subagent a way to check its own output before returning it. They also give the coordinator a way to check the result. That's the second half of the example: the same criteria, written as code.
e0e18e889b:
One boundary to keep clear. "Goals, not procedures" doesn't mean "never specify an order".

Some steps are hard requirements: verify the customer's identity before a refund, run the linter before committing. That isn't guidance for a capable agent. It's a rule, and chapter 03 puts rules in code (hooks and gates), where they hold every time.

The brief carries the part that benefits from judgment. Code carries the part that must not vary.
a2fc77df49: Put the three skills together with the scope and format fields from earlier sections, and the brief has a fixed anatomy. The companion TaskBrief class renders it and refuses incomplete briefs. That turns a prompt-writing habit into a property you can unit-test.
3dd3d143e0:
The exam guide's sample for this task statement describes a research system asked for a report on the impact of AI on creative industries. The final report covers only visual arts.

The logs show the coordinator created subtasks named something like "AI image generators", "AI in graphic design" and "AI in digital illustration". Each subagent completed its subtask well. The question asks where the root cause lies, and the answer is the coordinator's decomposition.

The reasoning is the part to internalise. When every component reports success and the output is still wrong, look at the step that defined the work. A component can only be correct relative to the task it was given.
c93b5158f4: Companion example 07_narrow_decomposition.py reproduces it with a coverage map of five areas: visual art, music, film and TV, writing, games. Run A uses the narrow decomposition from the sample. Run B enumerates the sub-domains first:
5076e99515:
Study the first run's second line: zero errors anywhere in the trace. Nothing in the logs, the subagent results or the token counts signals a problem. The defect shows only when you compare what was covered against a map of what the topic contains. In run A, that comparison happens only because the example computes it.

The lesson for your own systems has three parts.

  • Put the enumeration in the coordinator prompt: "before delegating, list the sub-domains of the topic and check that your subtasks together cover the whole question".
  • Make coverage checkable: have each subagent return a field naming the sub-area it covered. The coordinator (or a test) can then compare covered against expected, as the example's covered() does.
  • Close the loop: when the check finds a gap, the coordinator re-delegates it (section 11).

Several things don't fix the problem. A larger model for the subagents won't (they were correct). Neither will a better search tool (they found good sources), a stricter synthesizer (it merged what it received), or more instructions to the subagents about completeness (they can't know what their siblings were assigned).
eb8b034e27:
Narrowness has a mirror image. A coordinator can also split too finely: twelve subagents for a question with three real angles. Each one repays the fixed cost of a system prompt and tool list, and each returns overlapping material.

The sizing question is the one a Spring Batch designer asks about partition count. You want enough partitions to cover the input and use the parallelism, and few enough that overhead doesn't dominate. A decomposition is good when it's collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive at the level the question needs.
1b4aa9049e: Splitting into sub-areas isn't enough if the sub-areas overlap. Two subagents asked to research "AI in music" and "generative audio" are working the same ground under two names. The coordinator pays twice for the same sources. Example 08_partitioning_overlap.py measures it from the returned URLs:
119cd36d93:
Half the work in the first run is waste, and the waste hides. The merged report looks fine. Only the bill and the latency show the cost.

Partitioning means choosing non-overlapping dimensions and telling every subagent where its lane ends. The usual dimensions are the sub-domain (music, film, games), the source type (academic papers, industry reports, regulatory filings), the time window (before and after a policy change), and the region.

Each dimension suits a different question. A comparison across carriers partitions by carrier. A history partitions by period. A risk review partitions by source type, because the evidence differs in kind.

Then state the partition inside each brief with an out-of-scope line ("covered by other agents: ..."), which the TaskBrief renders. That line costs one sentence and does two jobs. It stops the subagent drifting into a sibling's territory. And it lets the subagent report "found something relevant to network quality; not my lane" as a note for the coordinator, instead of researching it.

Anthropic's own account of its research system describes the failure this prevents. Without clear boundaries, one subagent explored one reading of a vague task while two others duplicated work on another.
19b3ff1210:
The fourth coordinator job and the first skill on the list are the same idea. A coordinator should judge how hard the question is before deciding how many subagents to launch, and which ones.

  • A single fact (which source says churn rose after the price increase) needs one researcher and no synthesizer.
  • A question with several angles needs one researcher per angle, in parallel.
  • A comparison that needs both the company's own data and public sources needs researchers, the warehouse analyst and a synthesizer.

Example 09_selective_invocation.py runs three questions through three plans. Then it runs the simple one through a coordinator that always fans out to everyone:
1f38de0f9f:
In the example, the "judgment" is a rule in a scripted coordinator, because a fake can't reason. With a real model, it's the coordinator's decision, steered by the sentence you put in its prompt.

The shape of that sentence is a small rubric. One subagent for a single fact. One per angle for a multi-faceted topic. Specialists plus a synthesizer when the answer needs internal data and public sources, or an explicit comparison.

Anthropic's research-system write-up uses scaling rules of exactly this kind and embeds them in the lead agent's prompt. Without them, models tend to over-invest in simple queries.

Two more forms of dynamic selection belong here.

  • Selecting the type: the coordinator chooses between a web researcher and a warehouse analyst from their descriptions. That's why the descriptions carry "not for" clauses.
  • Selecting the model: the definition's model field lets cheap, narrow, high-volume work run on a smaller model, while synthesis and judgment run on a stronger one.

The exam's wrong answer is usually the fixed pipeline that runs every subagent for every query.
cdf26e368a: Independent sub-areas should run at the same time. You already know the mechanism from chapter 01. A single assistant response can contain several tool_use blocks, and the harness answers all of them in one user message. Applied to the Task tool, several Task blocks in one coordinator response means several subagents running concurrently. The wire shape is:
f78eb81ec1:
The next request carries three tool_result blocks, one per id, in one user message. Nothing about pairing changes.

The coordinator's loop doesn't resume until every subagent has finished. So its wall-clock time is set by the slowest subagent.

The input field names of the Task tool are an implementation detail of the harness (check the docs). The exam tests the pattern.
bbc9d10f9f: The alternative is a coordinator that emits one Task block per response. It looks the same in a transcript. Each subagent still returns a result, and the report is still right. But it serialises independent work. Example 06_parallel_vs_sequential.py runs the same three sub-areas both ways, with each simulated search taking about 150 ms:
17895b429c:
The last column of the trace is how you spot the problem in production: the number of Task calls per coordinator response. A run whose responses contain 1, 1, 1 for independent work has a coordinator prompt problem. The fix is one sentence: "launch independent subagents in the same response".

The exam phrases it as a symptom: "reports take six minutes; traces show the coordinator waits for each subagent before starting the next". It expects the answer "emit multiple Task calls in a single response". Wrong answers raise timeouts, change the model, or merge the subagents into one.
133e82b091:
Three cautions keep parallelism honest.

Independence is a property of the work, not a preference. Round 2 depends on round 1, because it needs the gaps. A synthesizer depends on every researcher. Those stay sequential. Launch together only what doesn't read each other's output.

Side effects need care. Research subagents are read-only, so concurrency is safe. Subagents that write files or call mutating APIs can collide, and the same idempotency discipline from chapter 01 applies.

Concurrency has limits. Model rate limits, harness caps on simultaneous subagents (check the docs for the current number), and your own budgets all bound how wide one response can go. If twelve sub-areas exceed the cap, use batches of independent Tasks per response, not one at a time.
5f085b7a78:
In the harness, the mechanics are what you'd expect. Python can map the blocks over a thread pool (the companion run_loop does, with ThreadPoolExecutor). A Java service uses virtual threads or CompletableFuture (section 15).

The one rule: results go back together, each carrying its own tool_use_id, in a single user message. Then a failed subagent is an is_error result among successful ones, rather than a missing result that causes a 400.
2faccae085:
The Agent SDK hides the mechanics, and an architect should have seen them once. Example 19_async_hub_and_spoke.py builds the whole hub with the Messages API shape and nothing else. It's short, because the pieces are the ones from chapter 01.

The coordinator is an ordinary loop. Its one tool is Task. The handler for Task is a coroutine that starts a second ordinary loop with a fresh messages list. The second loop's final text is the tool_result content for the first.

That's the entire idea of a subagent: a tool whose implementation is another model loop, and whose only output is a string.
8b27d23fe5:
Parallelism needs one line. When the coordinator's response contains four tool_use blocks, the loop runs await asyncio.gather(*[handlers[b.name](b) for b in calls]). The four spawn coroutines overlap while each one waits on the network.

A Semaphore around the body of spawn caps concurrency, and that's where a rate-limit budget belongs. gather returns results in the order of its arguments. So the results list lines up with the tool_use blocks without any bookkeeping, and the loop sends them back as one user message.

Every tool_use id gets exactly one tool_result, the same rule as in chapter 01. That's why spawn wraps its body in try/except and turns any exception into an is_error result carrying a small failure object.

Without that wrapper, one crashed subagent would raise out of gather. The other three results would be lost. And the next request would fail validation, because three tool_use ids were left unanswered.
703cb8428b:
The example runs in three scenarios and prints evidence that the fan-out is real and that failures stay inside the hub. The wall time of a run is about a third of the sum of the subagent durations. The four first-round starts fall within a millisecond of each other. And in both failure scenarios, exactly one coverage gap appears in the final report, labelled with the sub-area that failed.

One failure scenario is a structured failure reported by a healthy subagent (the search backend is down). The other is a crash of the subagent itself. The coordinator treats both as a gap to retry or report.

With a real key, you replace the async fake with anthropic.AsyncAnthropic(), and nothing else changes.
b78cbf95b6:
One round of delegation rarely finishes the job. Some sub-areas return nothing. Some rest on a single source. Some figures conflict. A coordinator that merges whatever came back and stops has made its first decomposition final.

The refinement skill is a loop at the coordinator level: evaluate the results against criteria, find the gaps, re-delegate only the gaps with the existing findings included, and repeat until the criteria are met.

It's the chapter-01 loop again, one level up. The stopping rule is the same too: a stop condition that comes from the state of the work, with a budget as a circuit breaker.
697dc9cc83: Example 10_iterative_refinement.py runs it on five FWA churn sub-areas, with the criterion "every sub-area has at least two independent sources". Here's the trace of the coordinator's evaluations:
d59a623432:
Walk through what the coordinator did.

Round 1 fanned out over all five sub-areas. Evaluation found two gaps: promo_expiry returned nothing, and customer_service had a single source.

Round 2 re-delegated only those two. For promo_expiry, it also reformulated the query, searching the topic under a name the sources actually use. That move only makes sense because the coordinator, unlike a fixed pipeline, can reason about why a search came back empty. It closed the gap. For customer_service, it passed the one known source so the subagent would look for different ones.

Round 3 tried again. The corpus simply has only one source, so nothing new arrived. The coordinator stopped and reported the gap instead of looping.

Three exits are visible in the code, and all three are required.
92829c574f: No progress. A round added nothing new, so stop and report what's unresolved. Without this check, a stubborn gap becomes an infinite loop of identical searches.
b26ca25459: Budget. A maximum number of rounds, set well above the expected, which stops the run and reports unresolved gaps. This is the circuit-breaker role from chapter 01 section 13. It triggers a report, never a silent return of partial work dressed up as complete.
d18df1a448:
Notice what the fixed-round version would have done. A coordinator written as "always do two rounds" would have stopped after round 2 with the gap still open. Or it would have run a pointless second round for a question fully answered in the first.

The exam's phrasing is "iterative refinement loops with gap evaluation". The contrast it draws is with a fixed number of rounds, or with a single pass.
5317bc629f:
A multi-agent run has more ways to fail than a single loop. The hub-and-spoke rule exists mainly so that every one of them lands somewhere that can do something about it.

Three kinds of failure occur at different depths.

  • Inside a subagent, a tool can fail. The subagent's own loop handles that exactly as chapter 01 describes: an is_error result, and the model adapts.
  • At the subagent level, the subagent may give up, run out of budget, or time out.
  • At the coordinator level, a Task call returns an error or an unhelpful result.

The coordinator can act on the last two only if the information reaches it in a usable form.
8541cd648b: Example 13_error_propagation.py makes the games researcher's search backend time out. It compares what the coordinator concludes under three subagent behaviours:
ba73542f2f:
The first line is the dangerous one. The silent subagent caught the timeout and returned an empty findings list with no gaps. That's indistinguishable from "searched and found nothing". The coordinator then wrote a confident, wrong sentence.

The other two runs show what structured failure context buys. The subagent's final message carries a failure object with a type, whether it's retryable, and what was attempted. So the coordinator can retry once, and either succeed or report a labelled gap.

It's the chapter 01 rule for tool errors, lifted one level: an empty result and a failed result are different facts and must look different.

Chapter 15 develops error propagation in full (access-failure versus valid-empty, partial results, coverage annotations). Here the point is the topology. In a hub-and-spoke design, exactly one place receives every failure. So there's exactly one place to write the policy: retry once, switch source, annotate the gap, escalate.
e274e1e9da:
The second benefit of the hub is that the evidence sits in one place. The companion harness keeps a coordinator-centred trace with five event types:

  • the model turn (with agent, stop reason and tokens);
  • the tool execution;
  • the Task start (subagent, label, prompt size, and inherited_messages: 0);
  • the Task end (duration and result size);
  • denials.

Example 05_hub_and_spoke_trace.py runs the full scenario: four parallel subagents, then a synthesizer. Its Task events:
86386c3c73:
This one log answers the questions an on-call engineer or an auditor will ask:

  • Which subagents ran, in what order, and whether in parallel (the start times).
  • How long each took, and how much it returned.
  • Which prompt each received (log the prompt, or at least a hash and length).
  • Which tool calls each made, attributed to the right agent.
  • Whether the synthesizer ran only after every researcher had returned.

The conflicting figures in the final report (1.4, 1.1 and 1.5 for the same metric) are visible with their sources, because the findings travelled as records. The runnable example asserts that the first-round starts are within 100 ms of each other, and that the report has a "CONFLICTING FIGURES" section.
f18758f157:
Two additions turn the event list into something you can operate.

The first is a run id plus span ids. Generate one short run id when the coordinator starts, and stamp it on every event. Give each Task its own span id, with the coordinator's span as its parent. A log search for the run id then returns the whole delegation tree, including events from subagents that ran concurrently and interleaved. The parent field lets you rebuild the tree without relying on timestamps.

In production, this is what an OpenTelemetry trace is, with the Task call as a span. The example uses plain JSON lines so the idea stays visible. Pass the run id to downstream services as a header, so a slow warehouse query can be traced back to the coordinator turn that caused it.

It's the same correlation-id discipline a telecom architect applies to an order flowing through a dozen services. The reason is the same, too: without it, you can't tell the logs of parallel branches apart.
c86d941020:
The second is cost attributed to the agent that spent it. Every response carries usage, so the trace can sum input and output tokens per agent label and multiply by a price table. Example 19 prints one row per agent: the coordinator, each researcher on the small model, and the synthesizer on the larger one.

Three things show up that a single total hides.

  • The coordinator is usually the largest line. It re-sends its growing history on every turn, and it receives every subagent's result.
  • A researcher that's expensive relative to its siblings is the first place to look for a bloated tool result or a brief that was too broad.
  • The price tier is visible. That makes the case for putting cheap models on the high-volume search work, and the stronger model on judgement, planning and synthesis.

The prices in the example are placeholders. Check the current pricing page before using any number for budgeting.
6a4454dcb4:
Three later chapters go deeper into the theory behind these controls.

  • Chapter 14 covers context preservation and escalation: what the coordinator should keep, summarise or drop as results pile up, and when a gap that retries can't close should go to a person.
  • Chapter 15 covers error propagation in full, including the structured failure object used here.
  • Chapter 16 covers human review, confidence calibration and provenance. That's the theory behind carrying source metadata through the merge.

This chapter uses only as much of each as the orchestration pattern needs.
0743cd511c:
In the real Agent SDK, the equivalents live in the message stream and in hooks.

Messages produced inside a subagent carry a parent_tool_use_id equal to the id of the Task tool_use block in the parent. So you can reconstruct the tree from the stream. The SDK also exposes SubagentStart and SubagentStop hook events (chapter 03 covers hooks), where you can write the start/stop records above.

By default, the stream forwards a subagent's tool calls and results, but not its text. An option forwards that too (forward_subagent_text in the version I checked). Example 15_sdk_options_offline.py builds synthetic AssistantMessage objects with the real SDK classes and shows the function that finds spawns:
49619f90c0:
The last item in task 1.3 isn't about subagents. It's about sessions, and it's easy to confuse with spawning, so start from what a session is.

In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, a session is a saved conversation. It's the transcript of messages (user turns, assistant turns, tool calls and results), written to storage under a session id. In other words, chapter 01's messages array, persisted.

That makes three operations natural.

  • Resume loads the saved history under the same id and keeps appending to it.
  • Fork loads the saved history, copies it into a new session id and continues there, leaving the original unchanged.
  • A fresh session starts empty, perhaps seeded with a summary you write.

The SDK exposes resume and fork as options: resume=<session id> and fork_session=True in ClaudeAgentOptions. The CLI has the equivalent --resume <id> with --fork-session (check claude --help for your version).
b8ac56c8b6:
The reason to fork is expensive shared groundwork. Suppose an agent spent twenty minutes and 60,000 tokens reading the order-service saga code and listing its failure points. Now you want two designs: a fix with an outbox table, and a fix that relies only on idempotent consumers.

Ask for both in the same session, and the second design is written by a model that has just read the first, and may be anchored on it. Start two fresh sessions, and you pay for the analysis twice. A fork gives both branches the analysed state and nothing from each other.

Example 14_fork_sessions.py proves the property with a model that reports whether it can see the other branch:
c52163b77c:
The scripted model appends the NOTE only when the other branch's text is in its history. That's a stand-in for the real effect, which is subtler: a model that has read a worked design tends to produce variations on it.

The code that builds the effect is small enough to show. It's worth reading, because it states the semantics exactly:
9144615027:
The same SDK also defines an offline fork_session(session_id, up_to_message_id=..., title=...) function. It copies a stored transcript into a new session with fresh message ids, optionally truncated at a given message. There are also options (resume_session_at) to resume only up to a message and branch from an earlier point in the conversation.

I confirmed these names in the installed package (version 0.2.164). Their exact behaviour is documented in the SDK reference. Check it before depending on details such as how a truncated fork treats an unfinished turn.
40a1e94da7:
A fork copies a conversation. It doesn't copy the world.

If both branches edit files in the same working directory, they're editing the same files. The second branch sees the code the first branch left behind, even though its conversation says otherwise.

For code work, give each branch its own checkout. A git worktree is the usual tool; check the Claude Code docs for its worktree support. Or restrict the branches to read-only analysis and design. The SDK has file checkpointing for rewinding edits in one session, but that's an undo mechanism, not isolation.

A fork also carries forward everything stale in the shared history. If the baseline analysis is wrong, or the files have changed a lot since, both branches inherit the staleness. The better move then is a fresh session seeded with a short, verified summary.
d617121ab7:
Subagents aren't free, and an architect should be able to say when they don't pay.

Each subagent re-pays a fixed cost: its system prompt, its tool definitions (the tool-use preamble, chapter 01 section 07), and the brief. Then it pays chapter 01's quadratic cost over its own short loop. The coordinator pays for the briefs it writes and the results it reads.

Against that, the single agent pays the quadratic term over one long history, in which every raw tool result stays and gets re-sent. The break-even depends on how bulky the tool results are and how many separate lines of work there are.

Example 17_cost_of_fanout.py measures it with the fake client's size-based token estimate, and a search tool that returns a page-sized blob around the useful records. Every figure below is an estimate; the shape is the finding:
ae0c4cb744:
Read the table in both directions.

At N = 1, the multi-agent design costs more than twice as much for no benefit. Spawning a subagent for a task one agent can do is pure overhead. That's the cost-side reason for selective invocation.

At N = 8, the multi-agent design is cheaper in total and keeps the coordinator's window small enough to reason well.

Two caveats make the table conservative or optimistic, depending on the case. If the single agent issued its eight searches as parallel tool calls in one turn, its history would grow once, not eight times, and its total would be much lower. And real subagents run several turns each, not the two in the fake.

Anthropic's research-system post reports that its multi-agent system used many times the tokens of a plain chat. It argues the quality gain justified that for high-value research. For a routine query, the same economics wouldn't hold. Tokens are the price of breadth. If the task is narrow, don't pay it.
1fa5b7e7bd:
Beyond cost, there are tasks where a coordinator and subagents are the wrong shape.

  • Tightly coupled work, such as a refactor where every edit depends on decisions made in the others, needs one agent with a shared context, or at least a strict sequential hand-off. Parallel subagents working from separate partial contexts make conflicting choices.
  • Small tasks don't repay the fixed cost.
  • Work that needs the user's earlier conversation is better done in the main session than in a subagent that starts blind.

A good rule: use subagents when three things hold. The work separates into sub-questions that can be answered independently. The tool output is bulky or noisy. And the answers can be summarised faithfully in a structured final message. Otherwise, keep one loop.
4d1cb85872:
Nothing in the pattern is Python-specific. For a Spring architect it's a familiar shape: a saga orchestrator that fans out to workers, joins their results, and compensates or reports on failure.

Two Java files are in the companion folder. java/CoordinatorFanOut.java has no dependencies, compiles with JDK 21 and runs under run_all.sh. It isolates the three harness properties that matter.

java/SpringCoordinator.java is a Spring Boot service over WebClient and Jackson, built on the chapter-01 loop. It needs WebFlux on the classpath, so it's reference code that run_all.sh doesn't compile or run.
a455583764: The record types mirror the wire. A TaskCall is a tool_use block named Task. A TaskResult is what goes into the tool_result, including a structured failure when the subagent errors or times out. The orchestrator executes all the calls of one coordinator response concurrently and returns the results in call order:
bb5e8ca006: The demo runs three stub subagents: one succeeds in 150 ms, one throws, and one is slow. Here's the output. The slow one is cut off by the 800 ms timeout and returned as a retryable failure, not as an exception:
6493797dbf:
Notice that the failed calls became data. The coordinator's next request would carry three tool_result blocks, two of them with is_error: true and a structured body. The model decides what to do: retry, narrow, or report.

Notice also that the constructor refuses an AgentDefinition that lists Task among a subagent's tools. That's the one-level rule from section 06, enforced where definitions are loaded.
c98cfc47bf:
The reference service has four pieces, and each maps to something you already do.

  • Definitions as configuration: an @ConfigurationProperties record binds agents.definitions.<name> from application.yml. Adding a subagent is a config change, reviewed like any other.
  • One loop method, called recursively: loop(agent, system, tools, allowed, firstUserText, budget, model) creates a new ArrayNode for the history on every call, so the subagent's context is fresh by construction. The coordinator calls it with the full tool set. The subagent calls it again from spawn() with the definition's own prompt and tools.
  • Permission as a set: execute() checks the tool name against the allowed set, and returns an is_error result when it's missing. The coordinator's set must contain "Task". A subagent's set is exactly its definition's tools.
  • Concurrency: all tool_use blocks of a response are submitted to a virtual-thread executor with CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, joined, and returned in one user message.
93ad817c87:
Three operational notes.

Put a bulkhead (Resilience4j Bulkhead or a bounded executor) around the subagent calls. Then one wide response can't exhaust your Messages API rate limit or your connection pool. This is the harness-side version of the concurrency cap in section 10.

Propagate the trace. Use one OpenTelemetry span per run, and a child span per Task call with the subagent type and prompt size. Below that, add child spans per model turn with stop_reason and tokens. Put the run id in the MDC so log lines from tools join the trace (chapter 01 section 17).

And keep the loop and the registry separate from the business tools. Then the fake in the test section can replace the HTTP layer without touching either.
f1325962ce:
As in chapter 01, the harness is deterministic even though the model isn't. So most orchestration bugs can be caught without a model at all. A scripted model plays a fixed sequence of turns, and the harness around it is real.

What you can pin down this way are exactly the properties this chapter has argued for:

  • a subagent receives one message, equal to the Task prompt;
  • Task is denied without permission;
  • independent subagents leave in one response;
  • failure comes back as data;
  • a brief missing its scope is rejected before it's sent.

Example 16_testing_orchestration.py has ten such tests, and they run in under a second. Four of them:
f5bbe704a9:
The remaining tests check six more things:

  • every task.start has a task.end (trace completeness);
  • the brief builder rejects a brief without scope or criteria;
  • a round-2 brief contains the prior findings verbatim;
  • an AgentDefinition with Task in its tools is refused;
  • a vague brief yields a labelled gap instead of invented findings;
  • the merge deduplicates by URL and flags conflicts.

Run them with python 16_testing_orchestration.py --mock.
e126d60d9c:
A scripted model can't test the part the exam spends most of its time on: whether the real coordinator decomposes well, writes complete briefs, and sizes the team to the question. Those are properties of a prompt and a model. They need evaluation with the real model, on recorded scenarios with graded outcomes.

For exactly the failures in this chapter, the grading can be cheap and mechanical.

  • For decomposition, keep a topic map per test question and score coverage: the fraction of expected sub-domains for which at least one finding exists. The covered() function in example 07 is the scorer.
  • For delegation, score brief completeness. Does every Task prompt in the trace contain the user's constraints, the scope line, the criteria and the format?
  • For selective invocation, record the number of subagents launched per question tier.

Keep the two kinds of test separate: deterministic tests for the harness, evaluations for the model. In a Spring project, the deterministic half is a WireMock or MockWebServer stub. It returns scripted responses to successive POSTs to /v1/messages, and you assert on the recorded request bodies.
1b5b081eea: The exam's wrong options are plausible engineering ideas. The table lists the ones this chapter has argued against, each with the mechanism of its failure. The three that most deserve a worked trace follow it. The others have their traces in the section named in the last column.
8a20037902: The temptation: "B needs A's output, so let B read A's mailbox directly and skip the coordinator hop". Example 18_antipattern_peer_to_peer.py builds it. Three agents (pricing A, network B, synthesizer S) share a queue. A crashes before publishing:
326f0d7acc:
Root cause. Three things were lost at once.

  • Evidence: A's failure is in a log nobody reads alongside the others.
  • Decision: B had to decide, locally and without authority, what A's silence meant. It chose the convenient reading.
  • Control: S merged without knowing anything was missing.

None of the agents was individually wrong. The topology gave no component the job of noticing.

Fix: the coordinator is the only component that sees every request and response. It receives A's failure, retries once, and tells S either the findings or the gap. The extra hop costs milliseconds. The missing hop cost a wrong report.
310b9a278b: The temptation: "give the researcher all the tools so it can handle whatever it meets". It looks like flexibility. Example 03_allowed_tools_task.py, part C, shows the failure in the harness with a restricted definition. The lint in example 04 shows what the unrestricted version looks like:
e848384ee0:
Root cause. A tool a subagent can see is a tool it may call. A web researcher that can query the warehouse will sometimes do so. The model reads its tool list and the task, and decides the warehouse might help.

Now internal data enters a context that was supposed to hold public sources. And a prompt injection in a fetched page has a path to an internal system. The specialty boundary that made the subagent easy to describe (and cheap to run on a small model) has dissolved.

A Task tool inherited by a subagent is the worst case. It can spawn work the coordinator can't see.

Fix: the definition's tools lists exactly the specialty tools, and the harness refuses anything else. You can see it in the trace: the call returns is_error, the denial is logged, and the model adapts.
d36df39178:
The CCAR-F exam presents a scenario and four options. For these task statements, the wrong options usually move the fix to a component that wasn't at fault. Or they smuggle in an assumption that the platform shares context automatically.

Work each scenario before reading the reasoning. Scenario 1 follows the official sample for task 1.2. Scenario 6 follows the shape of an official sample about a scoped verification tool, paraphrased, so use the official wording for your own practice.
6f0272ab2b:
Every subagent did what it was asked, and what it was asked covered one sub-domain. The defect is in the step that defined the work.

A is contradicted by the logs: the queries matched their briefs. B has no support, since there were no findings from other sub-domains to drop. D confuses capability with assignment; the subagents were correct relative to their briefs.

The fix lives in the coordinator prompt. Enumerate the topic's sub-domains before delegating, and check coverage against that list.
03235d4b22:
Spawning is a tool call. Without Task in the allowed tools, the call is denied or the tool isn't offered, so no wording can produce delegation.

A treats a permission problem as an obedience problem. C is doubly wrong. It doesn't fix the coordinator, and it gives subagents the ability to spawn, which breaks the one-level hub-and-spoke design. D changes the model to fix a configuration fault.
a4641e049c:
The subagent never had the first round's results. "We found earlier" refers to nothing it can see. The task prompt is the only channel in, so the information has to be written into it.

A misreads the problem as capacity; the window is empty, not full. B assumes a shared transcript the platform doesn't provide. D throws away the benefit of isolation and parallelism, and one long-running subagent would pile up noise.
6b202a182a:
Provenance is lost at the researcher's output, before the synthesizer sees anything. It can't cite what it never received.

B fixes the format at the source. It separates content from metadata, preserves the link through aggregation, and lets the synthesizer present conflicts instead of hiding them.

A asks for citations that don't exist in the input. C lets the synthesizer attach sources after the fact, which risks sources that don't support the claims, and it breaks the synthesizer's specialty boundary. D doesn't change the format.
fd8e2d4f7e:
The work is independent, but the coordinator serialised it by emitting one Task call per response. Multiple Task calls in one response run concurrently. Latency drops from the sum (six minutes) to roughly the slowest (two).

A addresses no observed symptom. C re-serialises the work inside one agent and fills one context with three areas. D changes the coordinator's speed, not the structure of the waits.
c84ada70cd:
It removes the round trips for the 85% case, while keeping the hub for the 15% that need real investigation. And it does so with least privilege: one narrow tool rather than a whole search capability.

B over-provisions. It collapses the specialty boundary and invites the synthesis agent to gather new, unsourced material. C verifies everything speculatively, including claims nobody ever questions, and it can't anticipate which claims synthesis will need to check. D is peer-to-peer messaging, which gives up the coordinator's observability and error handling.

Chapter 06 covers scoped cross-role tools in detail.
79b0070c15:
A fork gives each branch the analysed history and nothing from the other, and it leaves the baseline untouched.

A makes the second proposal conditioned on the first. B pays for the analysis twice. D is wrong because subagents inherit nothing automatically. Each would start blind unless the whole analysis were pasted into its prompt.

(If the branches also edit files, give each its own working tree.)
92e9b81c9e:
Done when:

  • you can draw the two nested loops of a delegation and say what crosses at each arrow;
  • you've seen a narrow decomposition pass every subagent check and still fail coverage;
  • you can rewrite any vague brief into the six-part form;
  • you know which of resume, fork, spawn and a fresh session fits a given situation;
  • every exam trap in section 17 maps to a mechanism you've seen run.
